title: Sliding Window
description: Learn to recognize, derive, implement, and analyze sliding window patterns.
learning_objectives: Derive an optimized solution from a naive baseline
Implement and analyze the pattern in Python

sections.title: Recognition and core idea
sections.markdown:
## When to recognize this pattern
Look for a contiguous subarray or substring maintained incrementally, repeated work, or a prompt whose constraints rule out a quadratic scan.

## Core idea
A sliding window represents one contiguous substring or subarray. The template for a fixed window adds the new right item and removes the old left item. A variable window expands right, then shrinks left while a monotone validity condition is violated.

```text
[2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2]
[-------]             first window
   [-------]          subtract outgoing 2, add incoming 1
```
key_points: Recognition: a contiguous subarray or substring maintained incrementally.
State the invariant before choosing code.

sections.title: From naive to better
sections.learning_objective: Derive the optimized approach from a baseline.
sections.markdown:
## Naive approach
Start with recomputing every candidate range. It may be easy to verify, but it repeats work and becomes too slow as input grows. State its cost before optimizing.

## Better approach
Use fixed window updates and variable window expand/shrink. The optimization is valid only if the invariant proves discarded work cannot affect the answer. Never quote a complexity without identifying the operation that dominates it.

sections.title: Python implementation
sections.markdown:
## Python implementation
The implementation below keeps the invariant visible and avoids clever shortcuts. Trace it before memorizing it.

## Step-by-step example
Use the shown input. Record the important pointer, state, or table after each iteration and verify that the final output is `9`.

examples.code:
def max_window_sum(nums, k):
    current = sum(nums[:k])
    best = current
    for right in range(k, len(nums)):
        current += nums[right] - nums[right - k]
        best = max(best, current)
    return best

print(max_window_sum([2, 1, 5, 1, 3, 2], 3))

sections.title: Complexity and common mistakes
sections.markdown:
## Time complexity
O(n) time. Explain whether sorting or preprocessing is included.

## Space complexity
O(1) auxiliary space. Input storage does not count as auxiliary space unless copied.

## Common mistakes
Using the pattern without its precondition, moving state in the wrong order, missing empty input, mishandling duplicates, and reporting average-case cost as a guarantee. For recursion, include call-stack space; for a DP table or hash map, count stored states.
